--- Page 1 ---
COMPASS: Composable Policy-Amortized Structured
Search for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
Nguyen Le Minh Hoang1
Van Duc Cuong12∗
Bui Trong Duc1†
Huynh Thi Thanh Binh1
1Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, Vietnam
2VinMotion, Hanoi, Vietnam
hoang.nlm2417125@sis.hust.edu.vn, cuong.vd220021@sis.hust.edu.vn
ducbt@soict.hust.edu.vn, binhht@soict.hust.edu.vn
Abstract
Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language
optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by
the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over
flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain
fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from
past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy
that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time
rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving opti-
mization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template
library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision
process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy
from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed
heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible
retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared
semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text
descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM
backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS
consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on
complex and mixed-category problems.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language optimization
problems into mathematical formulations and executable solver code. This setting, often referred to
as autoformulation, has the potential to lower the expertise barrier for building operations-research
models [Astorga et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025, Li et al., 2025]. However, optimization problems rarely
follow a single canonical pattern. A single description may combine routing, assignment, scheduling,
capacity, and resource-allocation structures, making correct template selection a central bottleneck
for downstream code generation.
Recent methods improve reliability by injecting structured modeling knowledge into the prompting
process. Autoformulation approaches decompose problems into variables, objectives, and constraints,
while structured retrieval methods organize modeling knowledge into hierarchical taxonomies [As-
torga et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025, Li et al., 2025]. Yet these retrieval strategies are typically fixed at
inference time. They can guide an LLM toward relevant modeling patterns, but they do not learn
from which templates previously led to valid formulations, feasible solver runs, or execution failures.
∗Co-first author.
†Corresponding author.
40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).
arXiv:2611.12060v1  [cs.AI]  9 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
In contrast, search-based methods can adaptively explore alternative formulations, but doing so
separately for each instance incurs substantial test-time cost.
This paper is motivated by the view that optimization-template retrieval is not only a semantic
matching problem, but a sequential decision process over structured modeling knowledge. Early
retrieval choices determine which modeling families and executable templates remain reachable,
so a good retriever should both exploit the organization of the template library and improve from
past modeling feedback. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework that represents the
template library as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and learns a traversal policy from LLM-based
structural judgments and solver-execution signals. By scoring problem-template compatibility in a
shared semantic space, COMPASS can evaluate newly inserted templates from their textual metadata
without changing the policy architecture, while beam traversal enables retrieval of complementary
templates for mixed-structure problems.
Our main contributions are:
• We recast optimization-template retrieval as a graph-structured sequential decision problem
over a template DAG, where internal nodes represent modeling families and leaves represent
executable templates. The DAG captures shared substructures among optimization models
and allows a template to belong to multiple related modeling paths, making the retrieval
structure more flexible than a strict tree taxonomy.
• We develop a policy-amortized retrieval algorithm that learns reusable traversal decisions
from LLM-based structural judgment and solver-execution feedback. The method uses
semantic node scoring to evaluate candidate templates from textual metadata, enabling new
templates to be inserted without redefining the policy output space.
• We empirically validate COMPASS across multiple optimization-modeling benchmarks and
LLM backbones, demonstrating consistent improvements over direct prompting, heuristic
structured retrieval, and test-time search baselines, with the largest gains on structurally
complex problems.
2
Related Work
LLM-based optimization modeling has recently advanced through autoformulation, structured re-
trieval, and feedback-guided search [Van Chien et al., 2026]. AutoFormulator explores the formulation
space with MCTS and symbolic pruning [Astorga et al., 2025], SolverLLM uses test-time MCTS with
dynamic expansion, prompt backpropagation, and uncertainty-aware feedback [Li et al., 2025], and
OptiTree retrieves modeling thoughts from a hierarchical OR taxonomy [Liu et al., 2025]. Related
systems extend this direction to mathematical modeling and OR reasoning, including MATHMO
for sequential decision-making under uncertainty [Liu and van der Schaar, 2026], StepORLM for
reinforcement learning and generative process supervision [Zhou et al., 2026], and operator-theoretic
autoformulation for Bellman-equation operator graphs [Baillet et al., 2026]. Beyond autoformulation,
LLMs have also been used as optimizers or heuristic designers: OPRO performs optimization through
iterative prompting [Yang et al., 2024], ReEvo combines evolutionary search with LLM reflection [Ye
et al., 2024], and HiFo-Prompt improves long-term knowledge reuse in automated heuristic design
[ChentongChen et al., 2026]. More broadly, LLM reasoning systems use search, decomposition,
tool feedback, and memory to improve inference-time decisions, as in Tree of Thoughts [Yao et al.,
2023a], self-consistency [Wang et al., 2023], Auto-CoT [Zhang et al., 2023], least-to-most prompting
[Zhou et al., 2023], ReAct [Yao et al., 2023b], CRITIC [Gou et al., 2024], Self-Refine [Madaan
et al., 2023], and Reflexion [Shinn et al., 2023]. Retrieval-augmented and tool-using systems such as
Self-RAG [Asai et al., 2024], DSPy [Khattab et al., 2024], ToolLLM [Qin et al., 2024], DRAFT [Qu
et al., 2025], and ToolEVO [Chen et al., 2025] further show the value of grounding LLM behavior
in external evidence and execution feedback. In contrast to methods that rely on fixed traversal
rules, costly per-instance search, or prompt/tool optimization, COMPASS learns a reusable semantic
value function over a persistent template DAG, allowing structured optimization-template retrieval to
improve from solver and judge feedback while remaining efficient at inference time. More related
work is presented in Appendix B.

Figure 1: Overview of COMPASS. The template library is represented as a DAG, and retrieval is
performed through a learned traversal policy guided by semantic priors and execution feedback.
3
Methodology
We propose COMPASS, a retrieval-augmented framework for translating natural-language optimiza-
tion problems into executable solver programs. The core difficulty lies in formulation selection: before
solver code can be generated, the system must identify suitable modeling abstractions, variables,
objectives, and constraints. Since early formulation choices determine which templates and constraint
structures remain plausible, template retrieval cannot be treated as independent semantic matching.
Instead, retrieval should model the dependencies among successive formulation decisions. Figure 1
illustrates this formulation-selection process and shows how COMPASS connects graph-based re-
trieval, template composition, solver-code generation, and feedback-driven policy improvement.
Algorithmic details of the inference and training procedures are provided in Appendix D.
COMPASS represents the formulation library as a DAG rather than a flat set of templates or a
strict taxonomy. Each node denotes a modeling state with associated textual metadata, and each
edge specifies a valid refinement from a broader abstraction to a more specialized formulation.
This representation captures the fact that optimization models often share intermediate structures:
for example, routing, assignment, and capacity constraints may co-occur across otherwise distinct
problem classes. Allowing multiple incoming paths to a node enables such shared modeling patterns
to be reused without duplicating templates.
Given a problem description p, the system computes a semantic embedding x = ϕ(p) and evaluates
candidate graph nodes during traversal. The learned value function estimates the expected usefulness
of selecting a node with respect to downstream formulation quality, rather than relying only on local
textual similarity. A language-model semantic prior provides an additional compatibility signal when
execution feedback is sparse. The final retrieval procedure combines these scores within beam search
to identify one or more templates that can jointly support solver-code generation.
Training uses supervision from structural judgments and solver execution. After a retrieved template
is instantiated and evaluated, the resulting feedback is assigned to the visited trajectory, so both
terminal templates and intermediate modeling decisions receive credit. This mechanism converts
retrieval into an experience-driven policy over the graph: previous successes and failures shape future
traversal, while inference remains substantially cheaper than repeated per-instance search.
3.1
Structured Retrieval over a Formulation DAG
We organize the template library as a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E), where each node represents a
reusable formulation abstraction and each edge encodes a valid refinement relation between modeling
concepts. A retrieval trajectory therefore corresponds to the progressive specialization of a modeling
hypothesis: starting from broad formulation families, such as routing, scheduling, or resource
3


--- Page 4 ---
allocation, the policy moves toward more specific abstractions and eventually reaches executable
template nodes.
At each retrieval step, the traversal state is defined as s = (x, ϕ(v)), where v ∈V is the current graph
node, and ϕ(v) is the semantic embedding. The admissible action set is restricted to the children of
the current node, A(s) = C(v), where C(v) = {u ∈V | (v, u) ∈E}. This constrained action space
preserves structural consistency among successive formulation decisions and reduces the effective
search space relative to flat selection over all templates in the library.
The DAG representation plays a key role in modeling the non-mutually exclusive structure of
optimization knowledge. In contrast to a strict tree taxonomy, where each abstraction has a single
parent, a DAG permits multiple refinement contexts for the same formulation node. This is important
because modeling concepts such as capacity, precedence, assignment, and flow conservation often
recur across different optimization families. The resulting structure supports parameter sharing across
related formulations, avoids redundant template duplication, and defines a structured decision space
suitable for learning long-horizon retrieval policies.
3.2
Semantic Value Function
The traversal policy should remain valid when the formulation library evolves. To this end, COMPASS
represents both problem descriptions and formulation nodes in a shared semantic space, rather than
binding actions to fixed template identifiers. Let τ(·) denote the tokenization map, Fη a Transformer
encoder, and P a pooling operator. For a text sequence z, we define hz = P(Fη(τ(z))) and
ϕ(z) = hz/(∥hz∥2 + ϵ), where ϵ > 0 is a small constant for numerical stability. The problem
embedding and node embedding are given by x = ϕ(p) and ev = ϕ(mv), respectively, where
mv denotes the textual metadata associated with node v. For each candidate node v, its semantic
representation is projected into the policy space as rv = σ(Wpev + bp), where σ(a) = max(a, 0)
is applied elementwise. The semantic value function is then defined as Qθ(x, ev) = qθ([x ∥rv]),
where qθ is a scalar-valued neural function and [· ∥·] denotes vector concatenation.
This parameterization makes the traversal policy depend on semantic compatibility between the input
problem and candidate formulation node, rather than on memorized template indices. Consequently,
related formulations can share statistical strength, and newly inserted nodes can be embedded and
evaluated directly from their metadata without modifying the output dimension of the value function.
3.3
Inference: Value-Guided Traversal with LLM Regularization
At inference time, COMPASS selects child nodes using a score that combines the learned value
estimate with a language-model compatibility prior. For a candidate child c ∈C(v), we define
ψ(c | p) = Qθ(x, ec) + λℓ(c, p), where ℓ(c, p) ∈[0, 1] denotes the semantic compatibility assigned
by the language model and λ ≥0 controls the strength of this prior.
The language-model prior is used as a regularizer rather than as the main retrieval policy. Since
Qθ is trained from a finite set of execution trajectories, its estimates may be less reliable for rare,
underexplored, or newly inserted nodes. The prior ℓ(c, p) provides a zero-shot semantic signal
over optimization concepts and formulation patterns, while Qθ encodes task-specific experience
accumulated from previous solver executions. Their combination improves traversal robustness under
sparse feedback without reverting to costly language-model-driven search.
To handle problems with multiple interacting modeling structures, COMPASS performs beam
traversal with beam size k. The procedure maintains the top-k partial paths according to ψ and
returns a set of candidate leaves L(p). The beam width is selected on validation instances to balance
coverage and computational cost. This is especially useful for hybrid optimization problems whose
complete formulation may require complementary templates from different refinement paths.
The retrieved leaves are converted into templates and composed into a final formulation t⋆= µ({tv :
v ∈L(p)}), where µ denotes the template composition operator. The resulting formulation is then
instantiated into executable solver code.
4


--- Page 5 ---
3.4
Learning from Execution Feedback
We model DAG traversal as a deterministic finite-horizon contextual decision process. Each episode
starts from a problem embedding x = ϕ(p), follows a trajectory over formulation nodes, and
terminates with template instantiation, solver-code generation, and execution. For a terminal node
v, the reward is defined as R(p, v) = αRjudge(p, v) + (1 −α)Rexec(p, v), where Rexec measures
solver-level correctness and Rjudge assesses structural compatibility between the problem and the
retrieved formulation. This decomposition mitigates the sparsity of pure execution feedback by
providing an additional semantic signal when generated programs fail syntactically, numerically, or
due to incomplete constraints.
The optimal node-value function satisfies Q⋆(x, ev) = E[R(p, v)] for v ∈T and Q⋆(x, ev) =
γ maxc∈C(v) Q⋆(x, ec) otherwise, where T denotes the set of terminal nodes and γ mildly penalizes
unnecessarily long refinement paths. Bellman propagation assigns credit from terminal execution
outcomes to earlier modeling abstractions, allowing the policy to learn not only which templates
succeed, but also which intermediate decisions tend to lead to valid formulations.
We train the value network with temporal-difference learning. For transition i, the target is yi =
ri + (1 −di)γ maxc∈C(vi) Qθ−(xi, ec), where di indicates termination and θ−denotes the target
network. The training objective is L(θ) = Ei∼B[wiℓδ(Qθ(xi, evi) −yi)], where ℓδ(a) = 1
2a2 if
|a| ≤δ and ℓδ(a) = δ(|a| −1
2δ) otherwise. This smooth L1 objective improves stability under noisy
execution and judge feedback.
To improve sample efficiency, we use prioritized experience replay. Each transition is sampled
with probability P(i) = pαPER
i
/ P
j pαPER
j
, where pi = |∆i| + εPER and ∆i = Qθ(xi, evi) −yi.
The corresponding importance weight is wi = (1/(NP(i)))β/ maxj(1/(NP(j)))β. Prioritizing
high-error transitions focuses updates on underexplored or poorly estimated regions of the traversal
space, which is particularly important under sparse terminal rewards. Hyperparameters such as λ, k,
αPER, and β are selected on validation instances.
3.5
Adaptive Template Expansion
Execution failures can also indicate limitations of the formulation library, rather than only errors
in the traversal policy. To address this case, COMPASS allows the formulation graph to expand
when repeated failures suggest that existing templates do not sufficiently cover a recurring modeling
pattern. Expansion is enabled only after the retrieval policy has reached a minimum level of stability.
Specifically, we use the gate gt = ⊮(t ≥τmin)⊮(εt ≤τε), where t denotes the training step, εt
is the exploration rate, and gt ∈{0, 1} indicates whether expansion is permitted. This condition
prevents early exploration noise and unstable value estimates from producing redundant or low-quality
templates. Once the gate is active, persistent execution failures are treated as evidence of missing
formulation abstractions.
When expansion is triggered, the language model abstracts reusable formulation patterns from failed
instances and reference solutions, and proposes new template nodes with textual metadata. These
nodes are inserted into G and embedded through the same semantic encoder used for existing nodes,
allowing the value function to score them without changing its output space. Subsequent feedback
then determines whether the newly added nodes become useful retrieval targets. DAG expansion is
performed only on training instances.
Thus, COMPASS adapts along two complementary axes: the traversal policy improves through
execution-driven value learning, while the formulation graph evolves when the current template set
lacks sufficient expressive coverage. This converts template retrieval from a fixed-library procedure
into an adaptive structured search process.
4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setting
We evaluate whether COMPASS improves the reliability, compositionality, and transferability of
LLM-based optimization modeling through learned structured retrieval.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Benchmarks and backbones.
We conduct experiments on six benchmarks: NL4Opt (245 prob-
lems)[Ramamonjison et al., 2021], MAMO-Easy (652)[Huang et al., 2024], MAMO-Complex
(211)[Huang et al., 2024], LPWP (288)[Xiao et al., 2024], IndustryOR (100)[Xiao et al., 2024], and
OptMATH [Lu et al., 2025] (166) [Lu et al., 2025]. These benchmarks cover linear programming,
mixed-integer formulations, mathematical word problems, and industrial optimization scenarios,
providing a diverse testbed for heterogeneous and compositional modeling. We use DeepSeek-V3 and
GPT-5-mini as primary code-generation backbones, and evaluate transfer to Qwen-32B, LLaMA-8B,
and DeepSeek-R1. This setup separates the effect of retrieval from the choice of downstream.
Baselines.
We compare COMPASS with direct prompting, OptiTree [Liu et al., 2025], SolverLLM
[Li et al., 2025], and AutoFormulator [Astorga et al., 2025]. We also include DAG-Greedy, which
uses the same template library and generator as COMPASS but replaces the learned value function
with the LLM-derived prior. This baseline isolates the contribution of policy learning over the shared
DAG structure.
Metrics.
We report exact accuracy, which requires both successful execution and correct solu-
tions, and code execution rate (CER), which measures runtime validity independently of solution
correctness.
Research questions.
Our evaluation addresses the following questions:
• RQ1: Effectiveness. Does COMPASS improve accuracy and robustness over existing
LLM-based optimization modeling approaches?
• RQ2: Structured retrieval. How much does DAG-based structured retrieval contribute
compared to flat or unstructured retrieval?
• RQ3: Ablation. How does each component of COMPASS affect overall performance?
• RQ4: Sensitivity. How sensitive is COMPASS to key design choices such as beam width,
regularization strength, and replay configuration?
4.2
Experimental Results

Main results.
Table 1 evaluates whether policy-guided DAG retrieval improves LLM-based op-
timization modeling over direct prompting and existing retrieval baselines. Across most datasets,
COMPASS achieves the highest accuracy, with the strongest gains on structurally complex bench-
marks such as MAMO-Complex, IndustryOR, and OptMATH. With DeepSeek-V3, COMPASS
6


--- Page 7 ---
improves over the strongest retrieval baseline by 5.2% on MAMO-Complex and 3.1% on MAMO-
Easy. With GPT-5-mini, the gains are larger on several datasets, including 4.3% on MAMO-Complex,
3.3% on LPWP, 3.0% on IndustryOR, and 4.7% on OptMATH.
The results demonstrate a clear pattern: the advantage of COMPASS becomes more pronounced as
formulation complexity increases. Direct prompting and flat retrieval are more susceptible to early
modeling errors, which can propagate into invalid constraints or incorrect solver code. In contrast,
COMPASS performs progressive refinement over a compositional DAG, enabling intermediate
modeling hypotheses to be assessed before final template selection. The consistent gains over
reasoning-oriented LLMs further suggest that scaling reasoning ability alone is insufficient when
the retrieved formulation scaffold is inadequate. These findings substantiate our central premise
that optimization modeling is best treated as a structured retrieval problem. By learning a reusable
traversal policy from solver and judge feedback, COMPASS enhances formulation consistency and
final solver accuracy, particularly on problems requiring compositional modeling.

Generalization across LLM backbones.
We further evaluate whether COMPASS transfers across
generator families and model scales by pairing the same retrieval policy with Qwen-32B, LLaMA-8B,
and DeepSeek-R1. Table 2 indicates that COMPASS consistently improves over direct prompting
across all evaluated backbones, with particularly large gains for weaker generators, such as +50.8%
on MAMO-Easy with LLaMA-8B and +16.0% on IndustryOR with Qwen-32B.
These results suggest two conclusions. First, the learned retrieval policy transfers across model archi-
tectures, indicating that the benefit of structured formulation retrieval is largely backbone-agnostic.
Second, smaller generators benefit more substantially from DAG-guided retrieval, suggesting that
COMPASS serves as an external modeling scaffold that reduces the formulation burden on the down-
stream LLM. In addition, COMPASS achieves near-perfect code execution rates in most settings,
indicating that structured retrieval improves not only solution accuracy but also the syntactic and
structural reliability of generated solver programs.
To assess whether these gains are merely due to additional inference computation, we compare
COMPASS against repeated direct prompting under matched inference budgets. Increasing the
sampling or prompting budget alone does not recover the improvements obtained by COMPASS,
indicating that the gains arise from policy-guided formulation selection rather than brute-force
inference scaling.

Learned traversal versus heuristic retrieval.
We compare COMPASS with DAG-Greedy, a
controlled baseline that uses the same DAG, template library, and DeepSeek-V3 generator, but
replaces the learned value function with locally greedy traversal based only on the LLM-derived
prior. Table 3 shows that COMPASS consistently improves accuracy across all benchmarks, with the
largest margins on MAMO-Complex (+7.1%) and IndustryOR (+3.0%). Since the retrieval space
and generator are held fixed, these gains isolate the effect of learned traversal.

The comparison indicates that local semantic compatibility is insufficient for globally correct formula-
tion selection. DAG-Greedy can select plausible intermediate nodes while committing to refinement
branches that omit essential constraints or modeling structures. In contrast, COMPASS learns from
execution-level outcomes and judge feedback, allowing earlier traversal decisions to account for their
downstream effect on final solver correctness.
Statistical significance.
Table 4 reports paired McNemar tests on the MAMO splits. The improve-
ments are statistically significant on both MAMO-Easy and MAMO-Complex (p < 0.001), with a
particularly strong imbalance on MAMO-Complex, where COMPASS corrects 17 instances missed
by DAG-Greedy while losing only 2. Because both methods share the same templates and generator,
this asymmetry provides evidence that the learned traversal policy systematically resolves failures of
heuristic retrieval rather than benefiting from random variation.

Difficulty-stratified analysis.
Table 5 stratifies IndustryOR by difficulty. The advantage of COM-
PASS is concentrated on harder instances: while DAG-Greedy is slightly better on easy problems,
COMPASS improves accuracy from 55.0% to 80.0% on hard problems. This pattern indicates that
local heuristic traversal is adequate for shallow formulations, but becomes less reliable when the
problem requires multiple interacting modeling choices. Learned traversal is therefore most beneficial
when early decisions have long-range effects on the final formulation.

Generation reliability.
Table 6 compares code execution rate in addition to accuracy. COMPASS
attains nearly perfect CER across all evaluated datasets, but the accuracy gains are larger than the
execution-rate differences, especially on MAMO-Complex. This distinction suggests that the main
benefit is not merely improved syntactic executability. Instead, policy-guided retrieval also improves
the mathematical correctness of the generated optimization formulations.
Component ablations.
Table 7 isolates the contribution of each design component. Removing
learned traversal causes the largest degradation, especially on MAMO-Complex, where accuracy
drops from 61.6% to 54.5%. This confirms that the primary improvement comes from policy-
guided navigation over the DAG, rather than from the template library alone. Removing the LLM

prior also reduces accuracy across datasets, indicating that semantic regularization complements
execution-trained value estimation, particularly when feedback is sparse.
The beam ablation shows that single-path retrieval is insufficient for many optimization problems, as
restricting traversal to K = 1 consistently weakens performance. This suggests that several instances
require combining multiple formulation patterns. Guarded DAG expansion also contributes positively,
especially on MAMO-Complex and OptMATH, suggesting that controlled template growth improves
coverage of missing modeling structures without introducing early noisy expansions. Overall, the
ablations indicate that COMPASS’s performance arises from the interaction of learned long-horizon
traversal, semantic regularization, compositional retrieval, and adaptive library expansion.
4.3
Sensitivity to Hyperparameter Settings
We analyze the robustness of COMPASS to key hyperparameters and use validation sweeps to select
the default settings used in the main experiments.
Soft LLM prior.
Table 8 evaluates the effect of the prior weight λ, which controls the interpolation
between the learned value estimate and the LLM-derived compatibility prior. Performance is maxi-
mized at λ = 0.3 across the three diagnostic datasets, and we therefore adopt this setting in the main
experiments.
Table 8: Effect of the soft-prior weight λ on accuracy (%) across three datasets using DeepSeek-V3.

The sweep reveals a clear bias-variance trade-off in traversal. When λ = 0, retrieval relies entirely on
the learned value function and loses zero-shot semantic guidance in underexplored regions of the
graph. Conversely, large values overemphasize the LLM prior and move the policy closer to heuristic
semantic traversal. The intermediate setting λ = 0.3 provides the strongest balance, indicating that
the LLM prior is most effective as a lightweight regularizer rather than as the dominant decision
signal.
Beam width.
Table 9 studies the beam width K used during DAG traversal. The best overall
performance is obtained with K = 2, which provides limited retrieval diversity while preserving
structural precision. A beam width of K = 1 restricts retrieval to a single refinement path and
therefore weakens the ability to combine complementary modeling patterns. However, wider beams
introduce noisy or mutually inconsistent templates, causing substantial degradation at K = 4. These

results indicate that optimization modeling benefits from controlled compositional retrieval, rather
than greedy single-path selection or overly broad exploration.
5
Conclusion
This paper introduced COMPASS, a framework that treats optimization-template retrieval as a
structured sequential decision problem rather than a one-shot prompting or ranking procedure. By
representing the template library as a compositional DAG, COMPASS learns reusable traversal
policies from solver-execution feedback and LLM-based structural judgments. The framework
combines value-guided retrieval, semantic regularization, beam-based template composition, and
adaptive template expansion to support robust formulation selection for LLM-based optimization
modeling. Empirical results across diverse benchmarks and LLM backbones indicate that retrieval
quality is a central bottleneck in optimization code generation. COMPASS achieves the largest gains
on structurally complex and mixed-category problems, where early formulation errors are difficult to
recover from during code synthesis. These findings suggest that learning how to navigate structured
modeling knowledge can provide gains beyond scaling the downstream language model alone. More
broadly, this work points toward adaptive optimization modeling systems that accumulate reusable
retrieval experience from execution feedback.

A
Limitations and Future Work
Although COMPASS is evaluated on multiple optimization benchmarks and LLM backbones, our
experiments cannot fully cover the diversity of real-world optimization tasks, solver interfaces, data
formats, and future language models. The selected benchmarks span different formulation types,
difficulty levels, and generator families, providing a broad but necessarily incomplete assessment of
the proposed retrieval framework. Extending the evaluation to larger industrial instances, domain-
specific solvers, and more heterogeneous problem settings is an important direction for future work.
LLM-based optimization modeling also remains sensitive to prompt design. Prompt variation can
affect problem interpretation, retrieved templates, and generated solver code. To reduce this source
of variability, all experiments use standardized prompt templates with fixed structure, as described
in Appendix E. Future work could study prompt-robust retrieval policies and adaptive prompting
strategies for more diverse deployment settings.
B
Additional Related Work
LLM-based optimization modeling.
LLMs have recently been used to automate optimization
modeling by translating natural-language problem descriptions into mathematical formulations and
solver-ready code. AutoFormulator explores the large formulation space with MCTS and symbolic
pruning [Astorga et al., 2025], while SolverLLM uses test-time MCTS with dynamic expansion,
prompt backpropagation, and uncertainty-aware feedback [Li et al., 2025]. OptiTree organizes OR
problems into a hierarchical modeling taxonomy and retrieves modeling thoughts through tree search
[Liu et al., 2025]. Related work further extends autoformulation to broader mathematical modeling
and dynamic decision-making: MATHMO treats modeling as sequential decision-making under
uncertainty [Liu and van der Schaar, 2026], StepORLM studies reinforcement learning and generative
process supervision for OR reasoning [Zhou et al., 2026], and operator-theoretic autoformulation
constructs Bellman-equation operator graphs for MDP and queueing problems [Baillet et al., 2026].
These methods show that structured search and feedback are crucial for optimization modeling,
but they typically rely on heuristic traversal or expensive test-time exploration. COMPASS instead
amortizes structured retrieval into a reusable policy over a persistent template DAG.
LLMs for optimization and heuristic design.
Another line of work uses LLMs as optimizers or
heuristic designers. OPRO casts optimization itself as prompting, where candidate solutions and their
scores are iteratively fed back to the LLM [Yang et al., 2024]. ReEvo combines evolutionary search
with LLM reflection to generate heuristics for combinatorial optimization [Ye et al., 2024], while
HiFo-Prompt introduces hindsight and foresight mechanisms to improve global control and long-term
knowledge reuse in automated heuristic design [ChentongChen et al., 2026]. In contrast, COMPASS
does not directly search over heuristic programs or solution candidates; it learns to retrieve modeling
templates that guide downstream solver-code generation.
Search, reasoning, and feedback in LLM systems.
LLM reasoning can be improved by exploring
multiple intermediate reasoning paths and using feedback to revise decisions. Tree of Thoughts en-
ables deliberate search over coherent reasoning states [Yao et al., 2023a], self-consistency aggregates
diverse reasoning paths [Wang et al., 2023], Auto-CoT automatically constructs chain-of-thought
demonstrations [Zhang et al., 2023], and least-to-most prompting decomposes difficult problems into
simpler subproblems [Zhou et al., 2023]. ReAct combines reasoning with external actions [Yao et al.,
2023b], CRITIC validates and revises outputs using external tools [Gou et al., 2024], Self-Refine
iteratively improves generations through self-feedback [Madaan et al., 2023], and Reflexion stores
linguistic feedback in memory for later trials [Shinn et al., 2023]. These methods mainly improve
inference-time reasoning, whereas COMPASS uses feedback to train a retrieval policy whose search
cost is amortized across future problems.
Retrieval, tool use, and adaptive LLM pipelines.
Retrieval-augmented and tool-using LLM
systems provide mechanisms for grounding and adapting model behavior. Self-RAG trains models
to decide when to retrieve and how to reflect on retrieved evidence [Asai et al., 2024]. DSPy ab-
stracts LM pipelines as optimizable computational graphs [Khattab et al., 2024]. ToolLLM studies
tool-use instruction tuning and API retrieval [Qin et al., 2024], DRAFT refines tool documentation
from execution feedback [Qu et al., 2025], and ToolEVO adapts tool usage under changing tool

Additional Experimental Details
C.1
Benchmark Matrix
Table 10 records the full study matrix targeted by the current scripts. It is included here so that the
appendix follows the RQ-organized experimental structure in the main text.
C.2
Training Hyperparameters
Table 11 summarizes the core hyperparameters used to train COMPASS. We use a fixed configuration
across all main experiments unless otherwise specified, with the soft-prior weight λ and beam width
K selected from the validation sweeps in Section 4.3. The configuration balances stable value
learning, controlled semantic regularization, and delayed DAG expansion, ensuring that template
updates occur only after the traversal policy has reached sufficient maturity.

--- Page 15 ---
C.3
Dataset Problems, Hardness, and Complexity
Table 12 summarizes the datasets used in our experiments. We distinguish modeling hardness from
conventional solver complexity. A benchmark may be challenging not only because the resulting
solver program contains many variables or constraints, but because the natural-language description
must be mapped to the correct decision variables, objective, constraint families, indexing scheme,
integrality assumptions, and, in many cases, multiple interacting formulation patterns. This distinction
is central to our setting: COMPASS aims to retrieve the appropriate formulation structure before the
downstream LLM instantiates it into executable code.
Table 12: Dataset characteristics. Instance counts are computed from the repository files. Hardness
refers to modeling hardness rather than solely to algorithmic solver complexity.

The benchmark suite spans a broad spectrum of retrieval difficulty. NL4Opt, MAMO-Easy, and
LPWP primarily assess whether COMPASS preserves the correct linear-programming scaffold
under varied natural-language descriptions. MAMO-Complex and OptMATH test deeper constraint
interpretation and symbolic consistency. IndustryOR provides the most compositional setting, since a
single instance may require several modeling families, such as routing with capacity and time-window
constraints or facility location with assignment constraints. This range is important for evaluating
structured retrieval: simple benchmarks verify that the policy does not degrade easy cases, whereas
complex benchmarks test whether learned DAG traversal improves over greedy or heuristic template
selection.
All datasets are evaluated under the same exact-accuracy criterion: the generated solver program must
execute successfully and return an objective value or solution accepted by the benchmark checker.
IndustryOR is further analyzed by easy, medium, and hard tiers in Table 5. The largest gains of
COMPASS occur on hard instances, indicating that learned structured retrieval is most beneficial
when modeling difficulty arises from interacting subproblem structures rather than surface-level
language variation alone.

Algorithm 1 COMPASS DAG Search for Template Retrieval
Require: Problem p, template DAG G = (V, E), root node v0, value function Qθ, prior weight λ,
beam width k
Ensure: Merged template t⋆, selected leaves L, traversal trace τ
1: function SEARCHDAG(p, G, Qθ, λ, k)
2:
x ←ϕ(p)
3:
B ←{(v0, [v0], 0)}, L ←∅, τ ←[ ]
4:
while B̸ = ∅and |L| < k do
5:
U ←∅
6:
for each (v, ρ, a) ∈B do
7:
C(v) ←{c ∈V : (v, c) ∈E}
8:
Append (v, C(v)) to τ
9:
if C(v) = ∅then
10:
L ←L ∪{v}
11:
continue
12:
end if
13:
Obtain ℓ(c, p) for each c ∈C(v)
14:
for each c ∈C(v) do
15:
s(c) ←Qθ(x, ec) + λℓ(c, p)
16:
U ←U ∪{(c, ρ∥[c], a + s(c))}
17:
end for
18:
end for
19:
B ←TopK(U, k)
20:
end while
21:
if L = ∅then
22:
L ←{v0}
▷fallback template
23:
end if
24:
t⋆←µ({tv : v ∈L})
25:
return t⋆, L, τ
26: end function
D
Algorithmic Details of COMPASS
This appendix summarizes the implementation of COMPASS. Algorithm 1 describes value-guided
retrieval over the formulation DAG at inference time. Algorithm 2 presents the training loop, including
reward construction, temporal-difference updates, guarded DAG expansion, and retry scheduling.

Algorithm 2 COMPASS Policy Training and Guarded DAG Expansion
Require: Training set D, template DAG G, replay buffer R, value function Qθ, target network Qθ−
Require: Reward weight α, prior weight λ, beam width k, expansion thresholds (τmin, τε), retry
queue Q
Ensure: Updated value function Qθ, template DAG G, replay buffer R
1: function TRAINCOMPASS(D, G, Qθ, Qθ−)
2:
for each training pass do
3:
for each instance (p, y) ∈D do
4:
t⋆, L, τ ←SEARCHDAG(p, G, Qθ, λ, k) with ε-greedy exploration
5:
Generate solver code from (p, t⋆) and execute the program
6:
Rexec ←1{checker accepts the output}
7:
Rjudge ←structural compatibility score for (p, t⋆)
8:
R ←αRjudge + (1 −α)Rexec
9:
for each transition (v, C(v)) in τ do
10:
d ←1{v ∈L}
11:
r ←R if d = 1, and r ←0 otherwise
12:
Store (ϕ(p), v, r, C(v), d) in R
13:
end for
14:
for each update step do
15:
Sample a prioritized mini-batch from R
16:
Update Qθ using the Huber temporal-difference objective
17:
if target synchronization interval is reached then
18:
θ−←θ
19:
end if
20:
end for
21:
if Rexec = 0 and t ≥τmin and ε ≤τε then
22:
Use the language model to propose a reusable missing formulation subtype
23:
Insert the corresponding template node into G and compute its embedding
24:
Remove redundant transitive edges from G
25:
Push (p, y) into Q
26:
end if
27:
if Q is scheduled for retry then
28:
Re-evaluate queued instances with ε = 0 and DAG expansion disabled
29:
end if
30:
end for
31:
end for
32:
return Qθ, G, R
33: end function

Prompts
E.0.1
Template Compatibility Scoring
Prompt
{Template Compatibility Scoring Prompt}
You are a mathematical formulator working with a team of optimization experts.
The objective is to tackle a complex optimization problem.
You are given a specific optimisation problem and a list of candidate template types.
For EACH candidate, rate how compatible it is with the problem on a scale from 0.0 to
1.0.
Scoring guide:
- 1.0 = The problem is clearly an instance of this type
- 0.7 = Strong match - most structural aspects align
- 0.4 = Partial match - some aspects overlap
17


--- Page 18 ---
- 0.1 = Weak match - only superficial similarity
- 0.0 = No match at all
Input problem:
{input_problem}
Current parent type:
{basic_type}
Candidate subtypes with descriptions:
{template_info}
Return the results in JSON format:
{
"ratings": {
"<subtype_name_1>": <float_score>,
"<subtype_name_2>": <float_score>
},
"reasoning": "<brief explanation of each rating>"
}

Subtype Identification and Formulation

- its current basic problem type
- the description of that type
Specific Problem:
{specific_problem}
Current Basic Problem Type:
{current_basic_problem_type}

{description_of_basic_problem_type}

E.0.9
Sample Problem Formulation Template
Prompt
{Traveling Salesman Problem Formulation and Gurobi Template}
You are a mathematical formulator working with a team of optimization experts.
The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a combinatorial optimization problem where a
salesperson must visit a set of cities exactly once and return to the starting
city while minimizing total travel cost.
Problem Description:
- Each city must be visited exactly once.
- The tour must return to the starting city.
- The objective is to minimize total travel distance or cost.
Key Constraints:
- Single Visit Constraint:
Each city is visited exactly once.
- Return to Origin Constraint:
The route must form a Hamiltonian cycle.
- Complete Tour Constraint:
All cities must be included without repetition.
Reasoning Flow:
1. Define binary decision variables x[i,j] indicating whether edge (i,j) is selected.
2. Minimize total travel cost:
sum(cost[i,j] * x[i,j]).
21


--- Page 22 ---
3. Add degree constraints:
- each city entered exactly once
- each city exited exactly once
4. Add subtour elimination constraints using MTZ formulation.
5. Add bounds on auxiliary variables.
6. Optimize the model using Gurobi.
Common Formulation Errors:
- Forgetting to forbid self-loops.
- Missing subtour elimination constraints.
- Incorrect MTZ indexing.
- Missing bounds on auxiliary variables.
- Confusing symmetric and asymmetric cost matrices.
Fixed Gurobi Template:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB
# Create model
model = gp.Model("TSP")
# Parameters
# cities
# cost matrix
# Variables
# x[i,j]
# Constraints
# visit constraints
# subtour elimination constraints
# Objective
# minimize total cost
model.optimize()
Return JSON only.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist
1. Claims
Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the
paper’s contributions and scope?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The abstract and Introduction state the method, scope, and empirical claims,
while the Experiments, Conclusion, and Limitations and Future Work sections provide the
corresponding evidence and scope qualifications.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims
made in the paper.
• The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the
contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or
[N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
• The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how
much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.
• It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals
are not attained by the paper.
2. Limitations
Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The paper includes a dedicated Limitations and Future Work section discussing
syntactic template merging, evaluation coverage across datasets and backbones, and prompt
sensitivity.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means
that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.
• The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.
• The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to
violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings,
model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors
should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the
implications would be.
• The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was
only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often
depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
• The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach.
For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution
is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be
used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle
technical jargon.
• The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms
and how they scale with dataset size.
• If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to
address problems of privacy and fairness.
• While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by
reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover
limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best
judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an impor-
tant role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers
will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.
3. Theory assumptions and proofs
23


--- Page 24 ---
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and
a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer: [N/A].
Justification: The paper does not present formal theoretical results. The equations and
algorithms define the COMPASS method and training objective, but no theorem, lemma, or
proof is claimed in the final paper.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.
• All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-
referenced.
• All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.
• The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if
they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short
proof sketch to provide intuition.
• Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented
by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.
• Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.
4. Experimental result reproducibility
Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main ex-
perimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions
of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The Methodology, Experiments, Appendix algorithms, prompt templates,
benchmark matrix, dataset discussion, and hyperparameter table describe the retrieval policy,
reward, training setup, evaluation metrics, and main run configuration. Reproduction with
closed LLM backends requires valid API access.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived
well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of
whether the code and data are provided or not.
• If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken
to make their results reproducible or verifiable.
• Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways.
For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully
might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may
be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same
dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often
one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed
instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case
of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are
appropriate to the research performed.
• While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submis-
sions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the
nature of the contribution. For example
(a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how
to reproduce that algorithm.
(b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe
the architecture clearly and fully.
(c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should
either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce
the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct
the dataset).
24


--- Page 25 ---
(d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case
authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility.
In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in
some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers
to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.
5. Open access to data and code
Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instruc-
tions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental
material?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: Our paper submission include the zip file with code and datasets to reproduce
main experimental results.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.
• Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/
public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.
• While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not
be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not
including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source
benchmark).
• The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to
reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https:
//neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.
• The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how
to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.
• The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new
proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they
should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.
• At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized
versions (if applicable).
• Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the
paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.
6. Experimental setting/details
Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperpa-
rameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The Methodology and Appendix specify the semantic encoder, value function,
replay buffer, reward blend, beam width, DAG-expansion gate, training passes, validation-
selected settings, benchmark counts, and core hyperparameters used in the experiments.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail
that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.
• The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental
material.
7. Experiment statistical significance
Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate
information about the statistical significance of the experiments?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The paired comparison against DAG-Greedy reports McNemar contingency
tables and exact binomial McNemar significance tests on MAMO-Easy, MAMO-Complex,
and the combined split.
25


--- Page 26 ---
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence
intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the
main claims of the paper.
• The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for
example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall
run with given experimental conditions).
• The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula,
call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)
• The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).
• It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error
of the mean.
• It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should
preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis
of Normality of errors is not verified.
• For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or
figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative
error rates).
• If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how
they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.
8. Experiments compute resources
Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the com-
puter resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce
the experiments?
Answer: [No].
Justification: The paper reports model backbones and experimental settings, but it does not
yet provide complete hardware, memory, wall-clock, or API-budget information for each
run.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.
• The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster,
or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.
• The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual
experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.
• The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute
than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that
didn’t make it into the paper).
9. Code of ethics
Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the
NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The work uses optimization benchmark problems and LLM APIs for solver-
code generation, does not involve human subjects, and documents limitations. No deviation
from the NeurIPS Code of Ethics is required.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of
Ethics.
• If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require a
deviation from the Code of Ethics.
• The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consid-
eration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).
26


--- Page 27 ---
10. Broader impacts
Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative
societal impacts of the work performed?
Answer: [No].
Justification: The paper focuses on technical methodology, experiments, and limitations, but
it does not include a dedicated discussion of both positive and negative societal impacts.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.
• If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal
impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.
• Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses
(e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations
(e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific
groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.
• The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied
to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to
any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate
to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to
generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out
that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train
models that generate Deepfakes faster.
• The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is
being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the
technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following
from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.
• If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation
strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks,
mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from
feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
11. Safeguards
Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible
release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models,
image generators, or scraped datasets)?
Answer: [N/A].
Justification: The paper does not release high-risk pretrained generative models, image
generators, or scraped datasets; it studies a retrieval and solver-code generation pipeline
over optimization benchmarks.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.
• Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with
necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring
that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing
safety filters.
• Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors
should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
• We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do
not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best
faith effort.
12. Licenses for existing assets
Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in
the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and
properly respected?
Answer: [Yes].
27


--- Page 28 ---
Justification: The paper cites prior work and names the benchmarks and LLM backbones.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.
• The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.
• The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a
URL.
• The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.
• For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of
service of that source should be provided.
• If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the
package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets
has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the
license of a dataset.
• For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of
the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.
• If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to
the asset’s creators.
13. New assets
Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation
provided alongside the assets?
Answer: [Yes].
Justification: The paper introduces COMPASS and documents the method through its
template-DAG representation, algorithms, prompt templates, hyperparameters, and evalua-
tion pipeline. Additional asset-level documentation would be needed if the code and DAG
files are released as standalone artifacts.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.
• Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their
submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license,
limitations, etc.
• The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose
asset is used.
• At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either
create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.
14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects
Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper
include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as
well as details about compensation (if any)?
Answer: [N/A].
Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing experiments or research with human
subjects.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research
with human subjects.
• Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribu-
tion of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be
included in the main paper.
• According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation,
or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data
collector.
15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human
subjects

--- Page 29 ---
Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether
such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB)

Answer: [N/A].
Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing, user studies, or other human-

Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research
with human subjects.
• Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent)
may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you

• We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions

Answer: [Yes].

Guidelines:
